facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: The financial base is sufficient to state the debt, earnings, cash flow and liquidity position of Builders FirstSource, Inc. at September 30, 2026, with the limitations listed under Gaps. Over the twelve months to September 30, 2026, reported earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization were well below FY2025 because gross margin fell and selling, general and administrative expense was broadly flat, while debt principal rose by 173.9 million, driven by 197.0 million of revolver borrowing. Total debt to EBITDA therefore moved from 3.26x to 5.15x and EBITDA to cash interest from 5.29x to 3.18x on the reported basis. Operating cash flow for the nine months to September 30, 2026 was 302.0 million against 1,021.1 million a year earlier, and the company repurchased 303.5 million of stock in the same nine months, almost all of it in the first quarter. Liquidity was 1,514.1 million at September 30, 2026 and stayed in a range of about 1.5 billion to 1.7 billion at the four balance dates read. facts.label: Interpretation
facts.text: - Leverage. Evidence: the debt table shows principal of 4,485,046 thousand at December 31, 2025 and 4,658,904 thousand at September 30, 2026, with the revolver drawn 197,000 thousand (Q3 page:13), while nine-month income from operations fell from 724,496 thousand to 244,113 thousand (Q3 page:2). Mechanism: the debt is largely fixed-rate notes with no scheduled principal payment before 2030, so leverage moves with earnings, and management attributes the gross profit decline mainly to a lower housing starts environment (R3 page:1). Implication: total debt to EBITDA is above the FY2025 level by about 1.9 turns on the reported basis, and further EBITDA decline raises it without any change in debt. - Coverage. Evidence: net interest expense for nine months rose from 206,139 thousand to 222,740 thousand (Q3 page:2), and cash interest for the twelve months is 284,752 thousand (C2). Mechanism: the 6.75% 2035 notes were issued on May 8, 2025 and so were outstanding for only part of the nine-month 2025 comparator, and the revolver was drawn in 2026 (K10 page:92, Q3 page:13). Implication: fixed charges are stable to rising while EBITDA is falling, which is why cover moved from 5.29x to 3.18x. - Cash flow. Evidence: nine-month operating cash flow of 302,031 thousand against 1,021,092 thousand (Q3 page:3), with working capital absorbing cash (Q3 page:28). Mechanism: receivables and inventories absorbed cash of 229,466 thousand and 122,131 thousand, partly offset by payables of 178,060 thousand (Q3 page:3). Implication: operating cash flow is already after cash interest, and free cash flow after capex of 150,875 thousand (C11) was positive but smaller than the repurchase of 303,519 thousand in the same period. - Liquidity. Evidence: availability of 1,459.1 million against a trigger of 173.2 million (Q3 page:27). Mechanism: availability is borrowing-base driven, so it follows receivables and inventory and can contract as sales fall; the borrowing base grew from 1,606.9 million to 1,731.7 million as receivables and inventory rose, which offset part of the 197.0 million draw, so availability fell only from 1,527.3 million to 1,459.1 million. Implication: liquidity is currently ample, but part of it rests on the same working capital build that reduced operating cash flow. - Maturities. Evidence: the maturity table above. Mechanism: no note or revolver is due before 2030 and the revolver and the 5.00% notes are both due in 2030, so refinancing risk concentrates in that year. Implication: no near-term refinancing pressure, with the 2030 date as the first test of market access.

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: Builders FirstSource, Inc. is a listed Delaware corporation that manufactures, supplies and installs structural building products for professional homebuilders and repair and remodel contractors, through roughly 575 locations in 43 states, organized into two geographic divisions reported as one segment. The business is cyclical and local: sales follow housing starts (net sales fell 2.2% in Q3 2026 on a lower housing starts environment), pricing is tied to service level and volume, and lumber is a commodity input and a sizeable sales category. The customer base is spread across large national production builders, regional and custom builders and contractors, so no single customer dominates, which supports revenue durability against single-name loss but not against a broad housing downturn, which is where 2026 stands. No sponsor, controlling shareholder, dividend recapitalisation or related-party leakage is documented in the sources. The transactions that matter to a creditor are the acquisition programme, the repurchase programme, the 2024 and 2025 senior unsecured note issues and the 2025 revolver amendment: together they explain why debt principal is higher while earnings are lower, as quantified in the financial handoff. Conduct is documented as shareholder-friendly through repurchases, and no creditor-adverse action is documented in the sources; legal capacity to distribute is limited by covenants whose terms are not supplied. The committee should treat what is missing as significant: the guarantor perimeter, the indentures and credit agreement, beneficial ownership and the end-market mix of sales.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: No transaction is pending, and no sponsor transaction, merger or refinancing was announced in the pinned sources between the end of the third quarter and the cutoff. The recent transaction history is in four parts. First, debt issuance: on February 29, 2024 the company issued 1.0 billion dollars of 6.375% senior unsecured notes due 2034, and on May 8, 2025 it issued 750.0 million dollars of 6.75% senior unsecured notes due 2035 at par, with the 2025 proceeds used to repay revolver borrowings [K10 page:92] "The net proceeds from the offering were used to repay indebtedness outstanding under the Revolving Facility." Second, the revolver was amended on May 20, 2025 to raise commitments from 1.8 billion to 2.2 billion dollars and extend maturity to May 20, 2030 [K10 page:92] "replace the existing revolving commitments of $1.8 billion with new revolving commitments of $2.2 billion, and to extend the maturity date to May 20, 2030". No new notes were issued in the first nine months of 2026; the revolver was drawn instead, with 197.0 million dollars outstanding at September 30, 2026 as set out in the financial handoff. Third, acquisitions: [K10 page:60] "During 2025, we completed a number of acquisitions for a combined $1.1 billion purchase price, net of cash acquired" across eight named businesses, then four more in the first nine months of 2026 for about 129.3 million dollars of consideration [Q3 page:9] "for a combined total purchase consideration of approximately $129.3 million", funded from cash and the revolver, with no pro forma information presented. Fourth, equity and strategic items: repurchases under authorizations renewed on April 30, 2025 and April 29, 2026, with 3.3 million shares bought for $302.9 million in the first nine months of 2026 and, per management, [R3 page:3] "The Company has $500 million remaining under its share repurchase authorization.", and a strategic investment in Digs, an AI platform, announced August 25, 2026 [Q3 page:22] "Under the partnership, the Company was the solo lead investor on Digs’ $25.3 million Series A financing". For each, the mechanics matter to a creditor: the note issues fixed the cost and pushed maturities to 2034 and 2035; the revolver amendment lengthened committed liquidity to 2030; acquisitions used cash and revolver capacity and added fixed cost and goodwill; repurchases reduce equity and cash; none changed the senior unsecured ranking. Key uncertainties are the covenant terms and guarantor perimeter, which the sources do not provide, and whether acquisition spending resumes at the 2025 pace.

facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: Builders FirstSource's fundamental credit position is weakening, with liquidity still ample. The strongest support is USD 1,514.1 million of liquidity at September 30, 2026 against a revolver covenant trigger of USD 173.2 million, no note or revolver maturity before 2030, and a diversified customer and supplier base. The weakest point is reported EBITDA of USD 904.402 million over the last twelve months, which lifts total debt to EBITDA to 5.15x from 3.26x and lowers EBITDA to cash interest to 3.18x from 5.29x. The outcome depends on the housing cycle and on capital allocation: further gross margin erosion, or repurchases and acquisitions funded while earnings are low, would use up the cushion that liquidity and the maturity profile provide. Category: Analyst Interpretation. Confidence: Medium.

facts.text: Thesis: Builders FirstSource is a scaled, diversified building products supplier whose reported leverage has risen to 5.15x as housing weakness reduced earnings, but ample liquidity and a first maturity in 2030 give it time, so the credit turns on whether margins stabilise (Analyst Interpretation; basis CP-1 leverage and liquidity figures, CP-1A credit translations on margin and cash-flow risk).

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Reported leverage has risen sharply. Debt principal at September 30, 2026 was USD 4,658.904 million against USD 4,485.046 million at December 31, 2025, an increase of USD 173.858 million driven by USD 197.0 million of revolver borrowing, while twelve-month reported EBITDA was USD 904.402 million against USD 1,377.708 million in FY2025. The debt is mostly fixed-rate senior unsecured notes with no scheduled principal payment before 2030, so leverage moves with earnings: total debt to EBITDA is 5.15x versus 3.26x and net debt to EBITDA 5.09x versus 3.12x (Documentary Fact, CP-1 leverage chart and calculations C5, C6). Management's own measure is lower, with net debt to Adjusted EBITDA at 4.08x on USD 1,129.1 million of Adjusted EBITDA, because add-backs of USD 224.7 million, mostly technology implementation expense, separate it from the reported basis (Management Language, qualified; CP-1 financial table and calculation C9). A committee should anchor on the reported basis until the add-back bridge is tested.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Coverage has narrowed but is not yet strained. EBITDA to cash interest is 3.18x on USD 284.752 million of twelve-month cash interest, down from 5.29x in FY2025, because earnings fell while the 2035 notes and the revolver draw raised interest cost (Documentary Fact, CP-1 interest cover chart). Operating income to net interest expense is 1.05x, which shows how little earnings remain after depreciation and amortization once interest is paid, so a further margin decline would move coverage on that basis below parity (Analyst Interpretation; basis CP-1 calculation C14).

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Cash generation weakened as working capital absorbed cash. Operating cash flow for the nine months to September 30, 2026 was USD 302.031 million against USD 1,021.092 million a year earlier, and free cash flow after capital expenditure was USD 150.875 million; nine-month repurchases of USD 303.519 million exceeded that free cash flow by USD 152.644 million (Documentary Fact; calculation C3 below). The filing lists the share repurchases and the USD 197.0 million of net revolver borrowing together and does not say one funded the other, so that link is an inference, not a finding (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 cash uses). The mechanism for creditors is that cash that could reduce debt went to shareholders while leverage rose.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Liquidity and the maturity profile are the main protections. Liquidity of USD 1,514.1 million is USD 55.012 million of cash plus USD 1,459.1 million of net revolver availability, far above the USD 173.2 million minimum at which the fixed charge test would apply, leaving USD 1,285.9 million of headroom to the trigger. No note or revolver matures before 2030, when USD 747.0 million falls due (the 5.00% notes and the drawn revolver), followed by USD 2,000.0 million in 2032, USD 1,000.0 million in 2034 and USD 750.0 million in 2035 (Documentary Fact; CP-1 liquidity, covenant and maturity sections). Two cautions apply: availability follows the borrowing base, so it can contract if receivables and inventory fall with sales, and qualified cash is counted in both cash and the borrowing base, so adding them may overstate liquidity by up to USD 21.3 million (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 liquidity basis).

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The business is diversified but cyclical. The ten largest customers took 14% of FY2025 net sales and the largest 4%, and the largest supplier was 8% of purchases, so concentration is not the main risk (Documentary Fact; CP-1A customer and supplier rows). Net sales fell 2.2% in Q3 2026 on a lower housing starts environment and gross margin fell to 27.8% from 30.4%, and the company states significant fixed costs, so volume and price pressure flow through to cash flow quickly (Documentary Fact; CP-1A volume driver, margin and cost structure rows). Management cites USD 60 million to USD 70 million of expected 2026 productivity savings, which is a management claim not tested here (Management Language).

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. First, Builders FirstSource has a diversified customer and supplier base, with low single-name concentration that limits abrupt revenue or supply loss (Documentary Fact; CP-1A customers and suppliers rows). Second, it has ample liquidity relative to its covenant trigger: USD 1,514.1 million against USD 173.2 million, with a revolver of USD 2,200.0 million commitments maturing May 20, 2030 (Documentary Fact; CP-1 liquidity and covenant sections). Third, its capital structure has no near-term maturity: fixed-rate senior unsecured notes mature from 2030 to 2035 and carry no scheduled amortization, which removes refinancing pressure until 2030 (Documentary Fact; CP-1 maturity chart). Fourth, management describes a leading position with competitive advantages from scale, service and a broad product offering; this is management's characterisation and is not verified (Management Language; CP-1A positioning and products rows). Fifth, reporting is regular and includes reconciliations, which helps monitoring, though the add-backs are management defined (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1A governance table).

facts.text: Weaknesses. First, reported leverage is 5.15x total debt to EBITDA and 5.09x net, up from 3.26x and 3.12x in FY2025, and cover is 3.18x, so there is less room for earnings declines (Documentary Fact; CP-1 leverage and cover charts). Second, earnings are cyclical with significant fixed costs, and the latest quarter shows volume and margin declines tied to housing starts (Documentary Fact; CP-1A volume, margin and cost structure rows). Third, shareholder returns and acquisitions continued while earnings fell, with nine-month repurchases exceeding free cash flow, which slows deleveraging (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 cash uses, CP-1A governance table). Fourth, earnings quality depends on add-backs: Adjusted EBITDA exceeds reported EBITDA by USD 224.7 million, and the technology implementation line is large and not itemised (Documentary Fact for the difference; Analyst Interpretation for its quality; CP-1 reconciliation, CP-1A gaps). Fifth, structural and covenant protections cannot be verified because the credit agreement, indentures, guarantor list and beneficial ownership are not supplied, and unquantified construction defect claims exist (Insufficient Information; CP-0 and CP-1A gaps).

Source-readiness review (CP-0) for Builders FirstSource, Inc. (issuer id bldr, NYSE: BLDR), as of 2026-11-05, evidence cutoff 2026-11-05. Pathway credit_snapshot, case kind public, current period Q3 2026 (quarter ended September 30, 2026), prior period FY2025 (year ended December 31, 2025), reporting currency USD. The filings print amounts in thousands of US dollars (financial statements) or millions of US dollars (release reconciliations and MD&A); no other currency was found in the pages reviewed.

Question answered: can the pinned source set support the selected downstream work (CP-1, CP-1A, CP-2, CP-5, the minimum module set), and what remains blocked? This module gives no credit conclusion and calculates no financial figure. It judges source sufficiency only; it does not judge completion of the downstream analyses.

The run context (sha256 26c088bea94d5b4a50b7398f335a28e56083f68ba3e62b9362de602502e2ae7e) holds the user's settings, not issuer evidence. It leaves borrower, parent, guarantors, ratings, quotes, deal terms, market valuation inputs, peers and research questions blank. Blank is not zero; each stays Not supplied.

### Extraction note on hashes

Each pinned file begins with a line "Visible text of <file>.htm, sha256 <hash>". Examples: K10 embeds 98a37e6dbf198c1f17c7e76d3c264be8e774be5ed8cb563bfa51ab28b40f9f5d and Q3 embeds 6474c9ad29f66248e8f92688fc59130dc8c0fc46859307d8a54a1f8197e45cd0. The pinned sha256 identifies the evidence used in this run.
## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| The seven pinned filings and releases cover the latest annual report and all three 2026 quarters for the single listed registrant, and support the four selected downstream analyses with stated limitations. No source is blocked. | Medium | The credit agreement, indentures and guarantor list are referenced but not supplied, so covenant and guarantor terms rest on filing summaries. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| The audited annual report, three quarterly reports and three earnings releases are present, period-labelled and on one consolidated perimeter. | Current-period and prior-period facts can be sourced from controlling filings. | High |

| Debt by series, revolver availability, letters of credit and a covenant-compliance statement are printed in each quarterly report. | Liquidity and debt can be sourced; covenant headroom beyond the availability trigger cannot. | Medium |
| The operating segments were realigned in the second quarter and prior-period product categories were reclassified. | Period-to-period comparisons need care about the basis used. | Medium |

| Adjusted EBITDA and the net debt ratio appear only in management releases, with reconciliation lines that differ from some reported lines. | Leverage on that basis is management attributed and needs reconciling to the filings. | Medium |

| No legal documents, guarantor list, presentations or fourth-quarter 2025 release are supplied. | Collateral, guarantee and covenant terms stay summary-level; structural analysis is limited. | Medium |
### Readiness view

The effective source set is READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS for each of the four selected consumers (CP-1, CP-1A, CP-2 and CP-5). No source is blocked and none is a fallback for a blocked source. The set contains the audited FY2025 annual report, the three 2026 quarterly reports and the three 2026 earnings releases, all for Builders FirstSource, Inc. as a single consolidated registrant. The limitations that every consumer must carry are: legal and financing documents are only listed as exhibits and incorporated by reference, not supplied; the guarantor subsidiaries are not named in any pinned source; Adjusted EBITDA and the leverage ratio are management-attributed measures that exist only in the releases; segment and product-category presentation changed during 2026; and the text extract flattens tables, so every figure must be checked against its page when used. A missing downstream analytical handoff is not a condition of readiness. The next evidence action is to read the debt note, the revolver availability table and the release reconciliations on the Q3 pages cited below, and to obtain the credit agreement, the indentures and the subsidiary list if covenant or structural work needs more than the filing summaries.
### Source assessment by document
#### Annual report K10

- Identity and perimeter: the registrant is the issuer itself, not a subsidiary in a combined filing. [K10 page:1] "BUILDERS FIRSTSOURCE, INC." and [K10 page:1] "For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025". The consolidated statements cover the Company and its subsidiaries; the Revolving Facility and notes are guaranteed by "Debt Guarantors" who are not named. [K10 page:93] "guaranteed jointly and severally by the Company and all other subsidiaries that guarantee our 5.00% 2030 notes".

- Authority and fidelity: audited statements with an auditor report dated February 17, 2026, which states [K10 page:71] "recognized consolidated net sales of $15.2 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025". The statement of operations is on K10 page:71, the debt note on K10 pages:92-95, leases and other finance obligations on K10 pages:95-96, subsequent events on K10 page:103 and the exhibit index on K10 pages:108-112.
- Coverage: Items 1, 1A, 7, 7A, 8, 9A and 15 are present (Item 1 starts [K10 page:2] "Item 1. Business"). The final chunk, K10 page:114, holds only a page number and no content.
- Version relationships: no amended 10-K is in the pack. The 10-K is the only audited source; its statement of operations is the FY2025 basis for the prior period.
- Reclassification: prior-year cash flow lines were combined to conform to current presentation. [K10 page:75] "have been combined with other non-cash adjustments".
#### Quarterly reports Q1, Q2 and Q3

- Q3 is the controlling source for the current period. [Q3 page:1] "For the quarterly period ended September 30, 2026". The same registrant and the same single consolidated perimeter apply to Q1 and Q2. [Q1 page:1] "For the quarterly period ended March 31, 2026" and [Q2 page:1] "For the quarterly period ended June 30, 2026".

- Statements: Q3 holds the statement of operations (Q3 page:2), balance sheet (Q3 pages:2-3), cash flows with cash paid for interest (Q3 pages:3-4) and the debt note (Q3 page:13). Statements are continuous across page breaks (the balance sheet runs from Q3 page:2 to Q3 page:3 and the cash flow statement from Q3 page:3 to Q3 page:4), so the reader must join chunks.

- Debt and liquidity: the debt table is [Q3 page:13] "Long-term debt consisted of the following as of:" with five fixed-rate senior note series, the revolver, other finance obligations and finance leases. Availability, letters of credit and the minimum-availability trigger are on Q3 page:27: [Q3 page:27] "Net excess borrowing availability on revolving facility" and [Q3 page:27] "Excess availability must equal or exceed a minimum specified amount, currently $173.2 million". Earlier thresholds are in [Q2 page:25] "Excess availability must equal or exceed a minimum specified amount, currently $180.1 million" and the Q1 equivalent on Q1 page:19.

- Covenant status: [Q3 page:13] "We were not in violation of any covenants or restrictions imposed by any of our debt agreements at September 30, 2026." The reported fixed charge coverage ratio itself is not printed in any pinned source; only the 1.00 to 1.00 springing test is described.

- Maturity schedule: the Q3 report contains no future-maturities table. The latest dated schedule is the FY2025 one at [K10 page:95] "Future maturities of long-term debt as of December 31, 2025, were as follows", which precedes the 2026 revolver borrowings and covers notes and revolver only.
- Revolver term: the Q3 report states the facility is [Q3 page:9] "revolving credit facility due May 20, 2030".
- Acquisitions: Q3 page:9 and Q3 page:10 list the 2026 acquisitions and give the fair-value table; pro forma information is stated as not presented, so no pro forma base exists in the pack.

- Segment change: Q1 describes three divisions as the operating segments, while Q2 and Q3 describe two. [Q3 page:6] "realigned its geographical divisional structure from three operating divisions (East, Central, and West) to two operating divisions (East and West)". The two are aggregated: [Q3 page:18] "We aggregate our two operating segments into one reportable segment". No segment-level figures are therefore available beyond the consolidated statements.

- Reclassification: [Q3 page:10] "As our product category alignment continues to be refined" the prior-period category net sales were restated; each 2026 quarter carries its own restated prior-period categories, so product-category history is not on one basis across Q1, Q2 and Q3.

- Subsequent events: no subsequent-events note was found in the Q3 report by searching "subsequent event" and "subsequent to". The latest dated event in the Q3 cover is the share count date. [Q3 page:1] "The number of shares of the issuer’s common stock, par value $0.01, outstanding as of October 23, 2026, was 107,606,319."
#### Earnings releases R1, R2 and R3

- Family and authority: management press releases furnished as Exhibit 99.1; attributed supporting claims that do not override filings. [R3 page:1] "Builders FirstSource Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results"; R1 page:1 and R2 page:1 are the first-quarter and second-quarter equivalents.

- Content: reported and adjusted figures, reconciliations, balance sheet, cash flows, product-category sales, guidance and an interest reconciliation. [R3 page:13] "Reconciliation of GAAP Net Income to Adjusted EBITDA" and [R3 page:13] "Interest Reconciliation". Product categories are on R3 page:14.

- Leverage statement: [R3 page:3] "net debt to LTM Adjusted EBITDA ratio of 4.1x" is a management statement. Adjusted EBITDA is not defined in any pinned filing: a search of K10, Q1, Q2 and Q3 for "Adjusted EBITDA" finds no occurrence, so the measure cannot be tied to an audited or reviewed definition.

- Add-backs: the reconciliation includes an unspecified line. [R3 page:13] "Other management-identified adjustments (1)" with the note [R3 page:12] "Primarily relates to severance, net gain/loss on sale of assets, and other one-time costs." The amount of each constituent is not given.
- Guidance: forward-looking guidance is given without reconciliation. [R3 page:4] "We are not providing a quantitative reconciliation of our forward-looking guidance".

- Presentations: no investor presentation is in the pack. The release points to one outside the pack: [R3 page:4] "accompanying presentation can be accessed". Releases serve in place of presentations; speaker notes and slide content are therefore not covered and are not claimed.
### Entity and instrument roles

| Borrower and note issuer | The Company is the obligor on the Revolving Facility and five senior unsecured note series, per the debt note | Resolved from the 10-K and Q3 summaries; credit agreement and indentures not supplied |

| Guarantors | "Debt Guarantors", defined as subsidiaries that guarantee the notes; not named in any pinned source | Unresolved gap |
| Restricted and unrestricted subsidiaries | The indentures restrict "designate unrestricted subsidiaries"; no designation list is supplied | Not supplied |
| Collateral | Revolver secured first on revolving collateral and second on notes collateral; notes senior unsecured | Summary only, from K10 page:93 and K10 page:94 |
### Consumer assessment
| Consumer | Status | Evidence demand and located coverage | Limitations carried |

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Reported EBITDA fell from FY2025 to the twelve months to September 30, 2026 while debt principal rose, lifting total debt to EBITDA from 3.26x to 5.15x. Liquidity is about $1.5 billion; no note or revolver matures before 2030. | Medium | Filings print no EBITDA, so it is built from reported lines; management Adjusted EBITDA is higher, and the fixed charge coverage ratio is not reported. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Twelve-month reported EBITDA is 904.402 million versus 1,377.708 million in FY2025; total debt to EBITDA is 5.15x versus 3.26x. | The leverage cushion thinned sharply within three quarters of 2026. | Medium |

| Cash interest over twelve months is 284.752 million; EBITDA covers it 3.18x versus 5.29x in FY2025. | Fixed charges absorb a larger share of earnings, raising sensitivity to further margin declines. | Medium |

| Liquidity at September 30, 2026 is 1,514.1 million: 55.012 million cash plus 1,459.1 million revolver availability; the springing covenant trigger is 173.2 million. | Near-term liquidity is large relative to the trigger; the fixed charge test is not currently applicable. | Medium |
| Senior notes and the revolver mature from 2030; the revolver and the 5.00% notes both fall due that year. | No refinancing wall before 2030, but 2030 holds both a note and the revolver. | Medium |

| Management Adjusted EBITDA of 1,129.1 million exceeds reported EBITDA by 224.7 million, mostly technology implementation expense. | Management leverage of 4.1x relies on add-backs; the reported basis is more conservative. | Medium |
### Financial base view

The financial base is sufficient to state the debt, earnings, cash flow and liquidity position of Builders FirstSource, Inc. at September 30, 2026, with the limitations listed under Gaps. Over the twelve months to September 30, 2026, reported earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization were well below FY2025 because gross margin fell and selling, general and administrative expense was broadly flat, while debt principal rose by 173.9 million, driven by 197.0 million of revolver borrowing. Total debt to EBITDA therefore moved from 3.26x to 5.15x and EBITDA to cash interest from 5.29x to 3.18x on the reported basis. Operating cash flow for the nine months to September 30, 2026 was 302.0 million against 1,021.1 million a year earlier, and the company repurchased 303.5 million of stock in the same nine months, almost all of it in the first quarter. Liquidity was 1,514.1 million at September 30, 2026 and stayed in a range of about 1.5 billion to 1.7 billion at the four balance dates read. The only financial covenant is a fixed charge coverage test of 1.00 to 1.00 that applies only if excess availability falls below a minimum; availability was far above it, and the ratio itself is not reported. The senior unsecured notes and the revolver are fixed in tenor, with the first maturity in 2030. The figures that most need a second look before use are the EBITDA definition (built here, not printed), the management Adjusted EBITDA that carries a large technology implementation add-back, and the guarantor perimeter, which no pinned source names.

Fair values at September 30, 2026 are printed per series (Q3 page:13). Notes are redeemable on terms in the indentures and carry a 101 percent change of control put; the indentures are not supplied.
### Covenants and definitions

- Maintenance test: the revolver has one financial covenant, a minimum fixed charge coverage ratio of 1.00 to 1.00 that applies only when excess availability falls below the specified minimum. [K10 page:93] "of 1.00 to 1.00 if our excess availability falls below the greater of $165.0 million or 10% of the maximum borrowing amount, which was $160.7 million as of December 31, 2025."

- Level at September 30, 2026: [Q3 page:27] "Excess availability must equal or exceed a minimum specified amount, currently $173.2 million, or we are required to meet a fixed charge coverage ratio of 1.00 to 1.00." Reported availability is 1,459.1 million, so headroom to the trigger is 1,285.9 million (C15). The same calculation gives 1,257.9 million at March 31, 2026, 1,379.7 million at June 30, 2026 and 1,362.3 million at December 31, 2025 against the 165.0 million then in force. The threshold moves with the borrowing base (10 percent of 1,731.7 million is 173.17 million).

- Reported figure: the fixed charge coverage ratio itself is Not supplied, because the test is not currently applicable and no pinned source prints a computed ratio. The definition of fixed charges and of the numerator is in the credit agreement, which is not supplied; the EBITDA used in this module is not that covenant definition.
- Compliance: [Q3 page:13] "We were not in violation of any covenants or restrictions imposed by any of our debt agreements at September 30, 2026."

- Negative covenants in the revolver and the indentures limit debt, liens, restricted payments, investments, asset sales and affiliate transactions (K10 page:93, K10 page:95); the baskets are Not supplied.

- Definition differences: reported EBITDA here (income from operations plus D&A) differs from management Adjusted EBITDA, which adds technology implementation expense, stock compensation, acquisition expense and other management-identified adjustments (R3 page:13), and from any covenant definition.
### Non-debt claims and commitments
- Operating leases: current plus noncurrent operating lease liabilities of 661,275 thousand at September 30, 2026 (Q3 page:3), outside the debt figure.
- Other finance obligations: inside the debt figure. [K10 page:96] "the Company is party to 110 individual property lease agreements with a single lessor as of December 31, 2025".

- Letters of credit: 75.6 million, under the revolver and already deducted from availability. [Q3 page:17] "As of September 30, 2026, we had outstanding letters of credit totaling $75.6 million under our Revolving Facility that principally support our self-insurance programs."

- Litigation: [Q3 page:17] "The Company has a number of known and threatened construction defect legal claims." The company states a reasonable possibility of loss that cannot be estimated; no amount is provided.

- Not found in the pinned sources by keyword search: pension or retiree medical obligations, factoring or supply-chain finance programs, purchase commitment tables, surety bond amounts. Their absence from the text is not evidence of nil; they are Not supplied.
### Management guidance, attributed

Management guidance is a management claim, not a filing fact, and is shown without reconciliation (R3 page:4 states none is given). [R3 page:4] "Adjusted EBITDA to be in a range of $1.075 billion to $1.125 billion." [R3 page:4] "Free cash flow of approximately $400 million to $450 million". [R3 page:4] "Interest expense in the range of $290 million to $300 million." [R3 page:4] "Total capital expenditures in the range of $175 million to $225 million."
### Recent events and cash uses

- Share repurchases: [Q3 page:5] "During the three months ended March 31, 2026, we repurchased and retired 3.3 million shares of our common stock for $302.9 million". Nine-month repurchases were 303,519 thousand (Q3 page:3) and the third quarter had none (Q3 page:32).

- Financing mix: [Q3 page:28] "Cash used in financing activities was $133.4 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, which consisted primarily of using $303.5 million for repurchases of common stock, partially offset by $197.0 million in net borrowings on the Revolving Facility." The filing states the two together; it does not say the borrowing funded the repurchases.

- Operating cash flow: [Q3 page:28] "The decrease in cash provided by operating activities was primarily driven by the decrease in net income in the current period compared to the prior year period, and an increase in net working capital in the first nine months of 2026."
- Acquisitions: [Q3 page:9] "for a combined total purchase consideration of approximately $129.3 million". Pro forma information is not presented.

- Equity investment: [Q3 page:22] "On August 25, 2026, we announced a strategic investment in, and collaboration with, Digs". Cash used for equity investments in the nine months was 27,578 thousand (Q3 page:3).

- Tax: a discrete income tax expense from an IRS research and development settlement affected the first half of 2026. [Q2 page:24] "we recognized a discrete income tax expense of approximately $43.9 million in the current year period".

- Interest rate sensitivity: [Q3 page:29] "A 1.0% increase in interest rates on the Revolving Facility would result in approximately $2.0 million additional interest expense annually". The notes are fixed rate.
- Subsequent events: none found after September 30, 2026 in the pinned sources; the 10-K subsequent event (the January 2, 2026 acquisition) predates the current period.
### Interpretation

- Leverage. Evidence: the debt table shows principal of 4,485,046 thousand at December 31, 2025 and 4,658,904 thousand at September 30, 2026, with the revolver drawn 197,000 thousand (Q3 page:13), while nine-month income from operations fell from 724,496 thousand to 244,113 thousand (Q3 page:2). Mechanism: the debt is largely fixed-rate notes with no scheduled principal payment before 2030, so leverage moves with earnings, and management attributes the gross profit decline mainly to a lower housing starts environment (R3 page:1). Implication: total debt to EBITDA is above the FY2025 level by about 1.9 turns on the reported basis, and further EBITDA decline raises it without any change in debt.

- Coverage. Evidence: net interest expense for nine months rose from 206,139 thousand to 222,740 thousand (Q3 page:2), and cash interest for the twelve months is 284,752 thousand (C2). Mechanism: the 6.75% 2035 notes were issued on May 8, 2025 and so were outstanding for only part of the nine-month 2025 comparator, and the revolver was drawn in 2026 (K10 page:92, Q3 page:13). Implication: fixed charges are stable to rising while EBITDA is falling, which is why cover moved from 5.29x to 3.18x.

- Cash flow. Evidence: nine-month operating cash flow of 302,031 thousand against 1,021,092 thousand (Q3 page:3), with working capital absorbing cash (Q3 page:28). Mechanism: receivables and inventories absorbed cash of 229,466 thousand and 122,131 thousand, partly offset by payables of 178,060 thousand (Q3 page:3). Implication: operating cash flow is already after cash interest, and free cash flow after capex of 150,875 thousand (C11) was positive but smaller than the repurchase of 303,519 thousand in the same period.

- Liquidity. Evidence: availability of 1,459.1 million against a trigger of 173.2 million (Q3 page:27). Mechanism: availability is borrowing-base driven, so it follows receivables and inventory and can contract as sales fall; the borrowing base grew from 1,606.9 million to 1,731.7 million as receivables and inventory rose, which offset part of the 197.0 million draw, so availability fell only from 1,527.3 million to 1,459.1 million. Implication: liquidity is currently ample, but part of it rests on the same working capital build that reduced operating cash flow.

- Maturities. Evidence: the maturity table above. Mechanism: no note or revolver is due before 2030 and the revolver and the 5.00% notes are both due in 2030, so refinancing risk concentrates in that year. Implication: no near-term refinancing pressure, with the 2030 date as the first test of market access.
### Source context and data quality

All figures are consolidated, in USD, for Builders FirstSource, Inc. and its subsidiaries. K10 is audited; Q1, Q2 and Q3 are unaudited; R3 is a management release. Where a filing and a release differ, the filing controls. Every pinned page was extracted successfully; tables are flattened to one value per line and statements run across chunk breaks, so each statement value above was read from its page and tied: FY2025 gross margin less selling, general and administrative expense equals income from operations of 786,276 thousand; nine-month 2026 and 2025 income statements foot to net income of 9,095 thousand and 403,719 thousand; 4,485,046 thousand and 4,658,904 thousand foot to the debt table lines; and net debt of 4,603,892 thousand equals management's 4,603.9 million. The 2025 comparatives used for the twelve-month figures come from the comparative columns of the Q1, Q2 and Q3 reports, because no 2025 quarterly report is in the pack.

### Business and transaction view

Builders FirstSource, Inc. is a listed Delaware corporation that manufactures, supplies and installs structural building products for professional homebuilders and repair and remodel contractors, through roughly 575 locations in 43 states, organized into two geographic divisions reported as one segment. The business is cyclical and local: sales follow housing starts (net sales fell 2.2% in Q3 2026 on a lower housing starts environment), pricing is tied to service level and volume, and lumber is a commodity input and a sizeable sales category. The customer base is spread across large national production builders, regional and custom builders and contractors, so no single customer dominates, which supports revenue durability against single-name loss but not against a broad housing downturn, which is where 2026 stands. No sponsor, controlling shareholder, dividend recapitalisation or related-party leakage is documented in the sources. The transactions that matter to a creditor are the acquisition programme, the repurchase programme, the 2024 and 2025 senior unsecured note issues and the 2025 revolver amendment: together they explain why debt principal is higher while earnings are lower, as quantified in the financial handoff. Conduct is documented as shareholder-friendly through repurchases, and no creditor-adverse action is documented in the sources; legal capacity to distribute is limited by covenants whose terms are not supplied. The committee should treat what is missing as significant: the guarantor perimeter, the indentures and credit agreement, beneficial ownership and the end-market mix of sales.

It combines the accepted financial figures (CP-1) and the business and transaction registers (CP-1A) for the current period Q3 2026 against FY2025, in USD. It quotes no source text, gives no peer ranking, instrument recommendation or recovery conclusion, and relies on the accepted upstream handoffs only.
## Sources

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Builders FirstSource's credit position is weakening but liquidity remains ample: reported total debt to EBITDA rose to 5.15x from 3.26x as housing weakness cut earnings, while no note or revolver matures before 2030. | Medium | Legal documents, guarantors, ownership and end-market sales mix are not supplied, and EBITDA is built from reported lines rather than printed. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Twelve-month reported EBITDA is USD 904.402 million versus USD 1,377.708 million in FY2025, lifting total debt to EBITDA to 5.15x. | Leverage tolerance is thinner; further earnings decline raises leverage without any new borrowing. | Medium |
| EBITDA to cash interest is 3.18x versus 5.29x in FY2025. | Debt service is still covered but with less cushion for further margin loss. | Medium |

| Liquidity is USD 1,514.1 million against a covenant trigger of USD 173.2 million; the first maturity is 2030. | Near-term refinancing and covenant risk is low, with 2030 concentrating notes and the revolver. | Medium |

| Operating cash flow fell and nine-month repurchases of USD 303.519 million exceeded free cash flow of USD 150.875 million. | Shareholder returns compete with deleveraging while earnings are low. | Medium |

| Customers and suppliers are diversified, but results follow housing starts with significant fixed costs. | Revenue loss from one customer is unlikely; a prolonged housing downturn is the main driver of default risk. | High |
### Credit view

Builders FirstSource's fundamental credit position is weakening, with liquidity still ample. The strongest support is USD 1,514.1 million of liquidity at September 30, 2026 against a revolver covenant trigger of USD 173.2 million, no note or revolver maturity before 2030, and a diversified customer and supplier base. The weakest point is reported EBITDA of USD 904.402 million over the last twelve months, which lifts total debt to EBITDA to 5.15x from 3.26x and lowers EBITDA to cash interest to 3.18x from 5.29x. The outcome depends on the housing cycle and on capital allocation: further gross margin erosion, or repurchases and acquisitions funded while earnings are low, would use up the cushion that liquidity and the maturity profile provide. Category: Analyst Interpretation. Confidence: Medium.
### Assessment
| Assessment | Category | Confidence | Basis |

| Weakening fundamental credit position with ample liquidity; leverage and cover have deteriorated within three quarters of 2026, while refinancing and covenant pressure are remote until 2030 | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | CP-1 leverage, cover, liquidity, maturity and covenant sections; CP-1A customer, margin, governance and credit translation rows |

| Confidence is capped at Medium: the CP-1A readiness for this module is READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS, legal terms are unsupplied and the EBITDA definition is built | Documentary Fact | Medium | CP-0 readiness view; CP-1A consumer assessment; CP-1 gaps |

Thesis: Builders FirstSource is a scaled, diversified building products supplier whose reported leverage has risen to 5.15x as housing weakness reduced earnings, but ample liquidity and a first maturity in 2030 give it time, so the credit turns on whether margins stabilise (Analyst Interpretation; basis CP-1 leverage and liquidity figures, CP-1A credit translations on margin and cash-flow risk).
### Key findings

Reported leverage has risen sharply. Debt principal at September 30, 2026 was USD 4,658.904 million against USD 4,485.046 million at December 31, 2025, an increase of USD 173.858 million driven by USD 197.0 million of revolver borrowing, while twelve-month reported EBITDA was USD 904.402 million against USD 1,377.708 million in FY2025. The debt is mostly fixed-rate senior unsecured notes with no scheduled principal payment before 2030, so leverage moves with earnings: total debt to EBITDA is 5.15x versus 3.26x and net debt to EBITDA 5.09x versus 3.12x (Documentary Fact, CP-1 leverage chart and calculations C5, C6). Management's own measure is lower, with net debt to Adjusted EBITDA at 4.08x on USD 1,129.1 million of Adjusted EBITDA, because add-backs of USD 224.7 million, mostly technology implementation expense, separate it from the reported basis (Management Language, qualified; CP-1 financial table and calculation C9). A committee should anchor on the reported basis until the add-back bridge is tested.

Coverage has narrowed but is not yet strained. EBITDA to cash interest is 3.18x on USD 284.752 million of twelve-month cash interest, down from 5.29x in FY2025, because earnings fell while the 2035 notes and the revolver draw raised interest cost (Documentary Fact, CP-1 interest cover chart). Operating income to net interest expense is 1.05x, which shows how little earnings remain after depreciation and amortization once interest is paid, so a further margin decline would move coverage on that basis below parity (Analyst Interpretation; basis CP-1 calculation C14).

Cash generation weakened as working capital absorbed cash. Operating cash flow for the nine months to September 30, 2026 was USD 302.031 million against USD 1,021.092 million a year earlier, and free cash flow after capital expenditure was USD 150.875 million; nine-month repurchases of USD 303.519 million exceeded that free cash flow by USD 152.644 million (Documentary Fact; calculation C3 below). The filing lists the share repurchases and the USD 197.0 million of net revolver borrowing together and does not say one funded the other, so that link is an inference, not a finding (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 cash uses). The mechanism for creditors is that cash that could reduce debt went to shareholders while leverage rose.

Liquidity and the maturity profile are the main protections. Liquidity of USD 1,514.1 million is USD 55.012 million of cash plus USD 1,459.1 million of net revolver availability, far above the USD 173.2 million minimum at which the fixed charge test would apply, leaving USD 1,285.9 million of headroom to the trigger. No note or revolver matures before 2030, when USD 747.0 million falls due (the 5.00% notes and the drawn revolver), followed by USD 2,000.0 million in 2032, USD 1,000.0 million in 2034 and USD 750.0 million in 2035 (Documentary Fact; CP-1 liquidity, covenant and maturity sections). Two cautions apply: availability follows the borrowing base, so it can contract if receivables and inventory fall with sales, and qualified cash is counted in both cash and the borrowing base, so adding them may overstate liquidity by up to USD 21.3 million (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 liquidity basis).

The business is diversified but cyclical. The ten largest customers took 14% of FY2025 net sales and the largest 4%, and the largest supplier was 8% of purchases, so concentration is not the main risk (Documentary Fact; CP-1A customer and supplier rows). Net sales fell 2.2% in Q3 2026 on a lower housing starts environment and gross margin fell to 27.8% from 30.4%, and the company states significant fixed costs, so volume and price pressure flow through to cash flow quickly (Documentary Fact; CP-1A volume driver, margin and cost structure rows). Management cites USD 60 million to USD 70 million of expected 2026 productivity savings, which is a management claim not tested here (Management Language).

Capital allocation and governance are shareholder oriented but not documented as creditor adverse. The company has no sponsor or controlling holder documented, pays no dividend, has repurchased shares under successive programmes since August 2021 and completed acquisitions of USD 1.1 billion in 2025 and about USD 129.3 million in the first nine months of 2026 (Documentary Fact; CP-1A governance table). No priming, uptiering, drop-down or collateral release is documented, but the sources contain no indentures or current reports, so absence is not confirmed (Insufficient Information; CP-1A governance and gaps).
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. First, Builders FirstSource has a diversified customer and supplier base, with low single-name concentration that limits abrupt revenue or supply loss (Documentary Fact; CP-1A customers and suppliers rows). Second, it has ample liquidity relative to its covenant trigger: USD 1,514.1 million against USD 173.2 million, with a revolver of USD 2,200.0 million commitments maturing May 20, 2030 (Documentary Fact; CP-1 liquidity and covenant sections). Third, its capital structure has no near-term maturity: fixed-rate senior unsecured notes mature from 2030 to 2035 and carry no scheduled amortization, which removes refinancing pressure until 2030 (Documentary Fact; CP-1 maturity chart). Fourth, management describes a leading position with competitive advantages from scale, service and a broad product offering; this is management's characterisation and is not verified (Management Language; CP-1A positioning and products rows). Fifth, reporting is regular and includes reconciliations, which helps monitoring, though the add-backs are management defined (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1A governance table).

Weaknesses. First, reported leverage is 5.15x total debt to EBITDA and 5.09x net, up from 3.26x and 3.12x in FY2025, and cover is 3.18x, so there is less room for earnings declines (Documentary Fact; CP-1 leverage and cover charts). Second, earnings are cyclical with significant fixed costs, and the latest quarter shows volume and margin declines tied to housing starts (Documentary Fact; CP-1A volume, margin and cost structure rows). Third, shareholder returns and acquisitions continued while earnings fell, with nine-month repurchases exceeding free cash flow, which slows deleveraging (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 cash uses, CP-1A governance table). Fourth, earnings quality depends on add-backs: Adjusted EBITDA exceeds reported EBITDA by USD 224.7 million, and the technology implementation line is large and not itemised (Documentary Fact for the difference; Analyst Interpretation for its quality; CP-1 reconciliation, CP-1A gaps). Fifth, structural and covenant protections cannot be verified because the credit agreement, indentures, guarantor list and beneficial ownership are not supplied, and unquantified construction defect claims exist (Insufficient Information; CP-0 and CP-1A gaps).
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity |

| Sustained housing weakness and gross margin compression | Volume and price declines on a significant fixed-cost base lower EBITDA and operating cash flow | Higher leverage and lower cover without new debt; main driver of default risk | Material |

| Leverage and cover erosion | Debt is largely non-amortizing notes, so leverage rises as EBITDA falls; cash interest is rising | Less tolerance for further decline; covenant not tested but earnings buffer thinner | Material |

| Capital allocation while earnings are low | Repurchases and acquisitions use cash and revolver capacity that could reduce debt | Slower deleveraging; creditor protection depends on covenant limits that are not supplied | Material |
